content:
Let’s break this down step by step.  

The first premise says:  
> Every ingredient of Moisturizing Bar is neither an ingredient of 31 EYE COLOUR nor an ingredient of VITAMIN E BB CREAM.  

In logical form:  
If \( x \) is an ingredient of Moisturizing Bar (MB), then \( x \) is **not** an ingredient of 31 EYE COLOUR (EC) and \( x \) is **not** an ingredient of VITAMIN E BB CREAM (VEB).  
\[
\forall x \, [ \text{MB}(x) \rightarrow (\neg \text{EC}(x) \land \neg \text{VEB}(x)) ]
\]

The conclusion says:  
> Whatever is none of this: an ingredient of VITAMIN E BB CREAM or ingredient of 31 EYE COLOUR, is an ingredient of Moisturizing Bar.  

In logical form:  
If \( x \) is **not** an ingredient of VEB and **not** an ingredient of EC, then \( x \) is an ingredient of MB.  
\[
\forall x \, [ (\neg \text{VEB}(x) \land \neg \text{EC}(x)) \rightarrow \text{MB}(x) ]
\]

The premise tells us:  
\[
\text{MB}(x) \rightarrow (\neg \text{EC}(x) \land \neg \text{VEB}(x))
\]  
But the conclusion reverses the direction:  
\[
(\neg \text{EC}(x) \land \neg \text{VEB}(x)) \rightarrow \text{MB}(x)
\]  

This is the **fallacy of affirming the consequent** in universal form:  
From \( P \rightarrow Q \), we cannot deduce \( Q \rightarrow P \).  

So the argument is **invalid**.

Final answer: invalid
